points.t: A raised, wandering, itchy serpiginous line on the foot, buttock or hand after tropical beach or soil exposure.
Animal (dog or cat) hookworm larvae burrow into human skin but cannot complete their life cycle, so wander in the epidermis.
Single-dose oral ivermectin or a 3-day course of albendazole (unlicensed; specialist or tropical-medicine advice); antihistamine for itch.
Secondary bacterial infection, and other migratory larvae (larva currens, *Strongyloides*) in the immunosuppressed.

points: Usual causes are **Ancylostoma braziliense** (dog/cat hookworm in the Americas and Caribbean) and *A. caninum*, plus *Uncinaria stenocephala* (European dog hookworm) and *Bunostomum phlebotomum* (cattle).
There may be tingling or prickling at the entry site within hours. The track appears **days to a few weeks** later. The larvae can lie dormant first.
**Sites:** **feet** (soles, toe webs, dorsum) most often, then **hands** (sand play, as in Case 2), buttocks, knees and trunk (sunbathing).

**Variants:** several tracks or loops, **vesicles and bullae**, and **hookworm folliculitis** (itchy follicular papulopustules, often on the buttocks). Look for eczematised or impetiginised skin from scratching.
The patient is systemically well. Rarely there is eosinophilia, or (with heavy infestation) Löffler-type pulmonary infiltrates.
The diagnosis is **clinical**: the typical migrating serpiginous itchy track plus barefoot exposure in a warm-climate setting.
No routine tests are needed. A biopsy is usually unhelpful because the larva is ahead of the track. Dermoscopy may show translucent segmental structures (the larval body) beyond the track.
Check for eosinophilia if the picture is atypical. Think of **Strongyloides serology** if the eruption is fast-moving, perianal/buttock or recurrent.

cards.name: Larva currens (Strongyloides stercoralis)
cards.clue: Moves **fast (up to 5–10 cm per hour)**, wide **urticarial** band, **perianal/buttocks/thighs/trunk**, comes and goes over months or years (**auto-infection**). The worm is a **human** intestinal parasite. Risk of **hyperinfection/dissemination with steroids or immunosuppression (HTLV-1)**. Needs serology/stool tests and ivermectin, and **must not be missed before steroids**

cards.name: Tinea corporis/pedis
cards.clue: Annular scaly expanding edge, does not "creep" daily; KOH positive

cards.name: Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis, phytophotodermatitis
cards.clue: Linear streaks fixed in place (e.g. lime juice + sun), no migration

cards.name: Jellyfish sting
cards.clue: Immediate painful linear whip marks after sea swimming

cards.name: Scabies burrows
cards.clue: Short (under 1 cm) grey burrows in web spaces/wrists; household itch

cards.name: Erythema migrans (Lyme)
cards.clue: Expanding annular erythema after a tick bite, not a thin track

cards.name: Impetigo / bullous insect bites
cards.clue: If bullous CLM: look for tracks

items.t: Rapidly moving perianal or buttock tracks (larva currens) or a patient on steroids: think *Strongyloides* hyperinfection.

pearls.t: Ivermectin tablets: give on an empty stomach with water (follow the product information). Counsel on mild transient GI upset and dizziness.
